texts: bad: two things go wrong. "a cold wind blows" casts the wind as a deliberate actor, which the translator reserves for things that move under their own power (a wind, like smoke or a tide, has to be the thing carried), and "unprepared lanterns" has nowhere to sit in the result clause, so the translator hoists the lantern up into the condition and the rule silently becomes a claim about every unprepared lantern anywhere. Both problems disappear if the wind acts on a lantern directly, the way your Cliff Path sentence does: "Whenever a cold wind from the sea strikes an unprepared lantern at night, the wind extinguishes that lantern."

good. the wind is acting on something, so it counts as a legitimate actor; the lantern is quantified in the condition where the rule can bind it; and "go out" is kept whole as a phrasal verb. This is the shape the other two sentences of this item should copy.

mixed: what is recorded is right - lanterns in shielded coves are safe from cold winds, asserted only for that setting - but "stay" is dropped, because a claim about a kind carries no occasion for a continuation to hold over. If the continuation is not essential, write "Lanterns in shielded coves are safe from cold winds.", which is exactly what the parse says; if it is essential, it needs a specific lantern and occasion, as in your "the lantern stays lit" sentence.
